lines: Picture a row of a table the ordinary way: every attribute of that one row sitting right next to each other on disk, in order.
Ask for that whole row back and the answer is almost embarrassingly simple. One contiguous slice of bytes, one read, done.
This is the layout nearly every database defaulted to for decades, and on this one question it's obviously the right call.
Row storage just won that question outright, so it's tempting to assume it's simply the better layout, full stop.
Here's the opposite question: not one whole row, but one single attribute, read across every row in the table.
Does the layout that just won the lookup also win when the access pattern flips around completely?
answer: It doesn't, and the reason is almost mechanical once you see it.

A row-major file has no concept of skipping just the attributes you don't want. To get to the next row's value of the one column you care about, a scanner still has to step past every other attribute in between.
That cost doesn't show up when you're reading one row. It shows up the moment you're reading one column, many times over.

lines: Here's that cost made concrete: ask for one column, across every row in the table, and watch how much of the file actually gets touched.
It isn't a slice of the file. It's the whole thing, because every attribute of every row sits in the path between one value of that column and the next.
The column you didn't ask for still has to travel through memory on its way past you.
So flip the layout completely: store each attribute in its own separate file, one file per column, nothing interleaved.
Now that same scan opens exactly the one file it needs and nothing else. The win is real and it's large.
But ask for a whole row back now, and you've traded one easy read for several separate ones, each from a different file, that then have to be joined back together into the row you actually wanted.
So neither extreme is free: one wins the lookup and loses the scan, the other does the reverse.

Here's the compromise a lot of real formats actually ship: keep a row's attributes together on the same page, the way row storage does, but inside that page, group each attribute's own values into their own little region.
A lookup still opens exactly one page, same as before. A scan still skips straight to the region holding the column it wants.
Here's the part that's easy to miss: this layout doesn't change how many pages get opened for a scan at all. The reader still has to visit every page the row-major version would have visited.
What changes is how much of each page, once it's open, is actually useful to the scan.
Same number of pages opened. A quarter of each one worth reading. That gap is the entire trick.
This is not a hypothetical compromise invented for a diagram. It's the actual shape of the file format that ended up winning the lakehouse.
A column-oriented file, where the compression and the encoding for one attribute can be tuned completely independently of every other attribute in the table.
That per-column tuning is only possible because the values of one column are already sitting together, grouped, inside the page — which is exactly the layout the last two steps just measured.
Three layouts, three honest trade-offs: keep rows together and you win the lookup but pay for every scan.
Split by column completely and you win the scan but pay for every lookup, with a join tying the pieces back together.

Group columns inside the page instead of across separate files, and you keep the page count of the first layout with the useful-byte ratio of the second. The next question is what survives when the reader and the writer no longer agree on the schema.
